# The laboratory data journey

Laboratory data pass through several scientific and operational stages before appearing in an NHANES XPT file.

```{=html}
<div class="specimen-journey">

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">1</div>
    <strong>Eligibility</strong>
    <span>Determine who qualifies for the examination or laboratory component.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">2</div>
    <strong>Collection</strong>
    <span>Obtain blood, urine, or another specimen under defined procedures.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">3</div>
    <strong>Handling</strong>
    <span>Process, label, store, and transport the specimen appropriately.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">4</div>
    <strong>Measurement</strong>
    <span>Analyze the specimen using a documented laboratory method.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">5</div>
    <strong>Quality review</strong>
    <span>Apply calibration, controls, flags, and analytical validation.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="specimen-step">
    <div class="specimen-step-number">6</div>
    <strong>Public release</strong>
    <span>Publish variables, documentation, weights, and analytical guidance.</span>
  </div>

</div>
```

::: {.callout-important icon="true"}
## The released value is the final stage, not the whole story

A laboratory result should be interpreted together with:

- who was eligible;
- how the specimen was collected;
- how the method worked;
- what units were reported;
- whether limits of detection applied;
- which survey weight represents the tested population.
:::

# Four laboratory-data principles

```{=html}
<div class="lab-principles">

  <div class="lab-principle">
    <h3>Methods matter</h3>
    <p>
      The same analyte may be measured using different instruments, procedures,
      calibration systems, or laboratory sites across survey cycles.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="lab-principle">
    <h3>Eligibility defines the sample</h3>
    <p>
      Not every participant is eligible for every laboratory component.
      Age, examination status, fasting, session, or subsample selection may apply.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="lab-principle">
    <h3>Units must be verified</h3>
    <p>
      A familiar variable name does not guarantee that units, coding,
      reporting limits, or interpretation remained unchanged.
    </p>
  </div>

  <div class="lab-principle">
    <h3>Provenance must survive</h3>
    <p>
      Every analytical record should retain its survey cycle, source file,
      component, variable origin, and processing history.
    </p>
  </div>

</div>
```

```{=html}
    <h3>Hematology</h3>

    <p>
      Hematology components may include complete blood count variables such as

    </p>

    <ul>
      <li>Review analyzer and method changes across cycles.</li>
      <li>Verify units and age-specific interpretation.</li>
      <li>Distinguish primary and repeat examinations.</li>
      <li>Retain specimen and cycle provenance.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div
    id="chemistry"
    class="component-panel"
  >
    <h3>Clinical chemistry</h3>

    <p>
      Chemistry components may include glucose, lipids, renal markers,
      liver-associated measurements, electrolytes, and other biomarkers.
    </p>

    <ul>
      <li>Determine whether fasting or examination-session restrictions apply.</li>
      <li>Review specimen type and analytical platform.</li>
      <li>Identify component-specific subsample weights.</li>
      <li>Check method-comparison or calibration guidance.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div
    id="exposure"
    class="component-panel"
  >
    <h3>Environmental exposure biomarkers</h3>

    <p>
      Exposure components may measure metals, pesticides, volatile compounds,

    </p>

    <ul>
      <li>Review limits of detection and substitution rules.</li>
      <li>Identify dilution adjustments where relevant.</li>
      <li>Check batch, specimen, and storage considerations.</li>
      <li>Confirm the applicable laboratory subsample weight.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div
    id="infectious"
    class="component-panel"
  >
    <h3>Infectious disease testing</h3>

    <p>
      Infectious disease components may include antibody, antigen,
      molecular, or other evidence of infection or immunity.
    </p>

    <ul>
      <li>Understand qualitative and quantitative result coding.</li>
      <li>Review confirmatory testing algorithms.</li>
      <li>Distinguish current infection, past exposure, and immunity.</li>
      <li>Check age and specimen-availability restrictions.</li>
    </ul>
  </div>

  <div
    id="nutrition"
    class="component-panel"
  >
    <h3>Nutrition biomarkers</h3>

    <p>
      Nutrition laboratory components may include vitamins, minerals,
      metabolites, and other indicators of nutritional status.
    </p>

    <ul>
      <li>Review fasting, supplement use, and collection timing.</li>
      <li>Check specimen stability and assay changes.</li>
      <li>Assess biomarker-specific reference considerations.</li>
      <li>Identify the appropriate survey weight and analytical sample.</li>
    </ul>

<script>
(function () {
  const buttons =
    document.querySelectorAll(
      ".component-filter"
    );

  const panels =
    document.querySelectorAll(
      ".component-panel"
    );

  buttons.forEach(
    function (button) {
      button.addEventListener(
        "click",
        function () {
          const target =
            button.getAttribute(
              "data-component"
            );

          buttons.forEach(
            function (item) {
              item.classList.remove(
                "active"
              );
            }
          );

          panels.forEach(
            function (panel) {
              panel.classList.remove(
                "active"
              );
            }
          );

          button.classList.add(
            "active"
          );

          const selectedPanel =
            document.getElementById(
              target
            );

          if (selectedPanel) {
            selectedPanel.classList.add(
              "active"
            );
          }
        }
      );
    }
  );
})();
</script>
```

# Anatomy of a laboratory variable

A laboratory variable should be understood through more than its short name.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Variable identity

Review:

- variable name;
- descriptive label;
- source file;
- survey cycle;
- component;
- specimen type.

## Measurement context

Review:

- analytical method;
- instrument or platform;
- calibration;
- laboratory site;
- specimen handling;
- quality-control procedures.

## Reported result

Review:

- unit;
- valid range;
- categorical coding;
- result flags;
- comment codes;
- missing-value conventions.

## Analytical population

Review:

- age eligibility;
- examination status;
- fasting requirements;
- subsample selection;
- valid survey weight;
- missing-result patterns.

:::

# Laboratory detection limits

Some laboratory components include values below a method’s detection limit.

The released data may provide:

- a reported result variable;
- a detection-limit indicator;
- a lower detection limit;
- an imputed or substituted result;
- cycle-specific analytical guidance.

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Do not invent a universal substitution rule

Rules such as:

```text
LOD / √2
```

or:

```text
LOD / 2
```

may be appropriate in some contexts but should not be applied automatically.

Use the component documentation, analytical objective, distribution, and sensitivity analysis to justify the treatment of values below detection.
:::

# Missing laboratory values

A missing result may indicate:

- the participant was not eligible;
- the participant did not attend the MEC examination;
- the specimen was not collected;
- specimen volume was insufficient;
- the assay failed;
- the result was excluded during quality review;
- the analyte was not measured in that cycle;
- the participant was not selected for the subsample.

The meaning of missingness should be investigated before excluding records.

# Laboratory quality and analytical quality

Laboratory quality assurance and data-analysis quality are related but distinct.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Laboratory quality assurance

May include:

- calibration;
- control materials;
- proficiency testing;
- instrument maintenance;
- reagent review;
- specimen acceptance;
- corrective action;
- analytical performance monitoring.

## Data-analysis quality assurance

May include:

- source validation;
- cycle tracking;
- variable harmonization;
- duplicate investigation;
- merge validation;
- missingness review;
- weight selection;
- reproducibility records.

## Shared objective

Both systems aim to ensure that:

```text
the reported result is accurate,
traceable,
interpretable,
and fit for its intended use
```

:::

# Common laboratory-data mistakes

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Mistake 1: Selecting a variable by name alone

The variable’s method, unit, eligibility, and cycle documentation must also be reviewed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Mistake 2: Assuming every participant has every laboratory result

Laboratory eligibility, examination completion, specimen availability, and subsampling affect record availability.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Mistake 3: Combining cycles without reviewing method changes

A consistent variable name does not prove analytical comparability.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Mistake 4: Ignoring detection-limit variables

Reported values near or below detection may require specific analytical treatment.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon="true"}
## Mistake 5: Using the wrong survey weight

The weight must represent the smallest eligible sample associated with the laboratory variables used.
:::

# Laboratory-data knowledge check

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Is a laboratory variable name sufficient to establish comparability across cycles?

No. Review the method, units, eligibility, instrument, documentation, and cycle-specific analytical guidance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why might a participant have no laboratory result?

They may have been ineligible, absent from the examination, missing a specimen, excluded during quality review, or outside the selected subsample.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Should repeat examinations be appended automatically to the primary laboratory file?

No. Their analytical role and eligibility must be investigated first.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What information should remain attached to an imported laboratory record?

At minimum, retain the survey cycle, source file, component, participant identifier, and file role.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Does a correct assay result automatically produce a valid population estimate?

No. Population inference also requires correct eligibility, data integration, survey weighting, and design-based analysis.
:::

# Laboratory-data checklist

Before analyzing an NHANES laboratory component, confirm:

- [ ] The correct component and source file are identified.
- [ ] The survey cycle is retained.
- [ ] The participant identifier is present.
- [ ] The meaning of one row is understood.
- [ ] Primary and supplementary records are distinguished.
- [ ] Variable labels and units are verified.
- [ ] Laboratory methods have been reviewed.
- [ ] Instrument or platform changes have been considered.
- [ ] Detection-limit variables have been identified.
- [ ] Missing-value meaning has been investigated.
- [ ] Eligibility criteria are documented.
- [ ] The correct survey weight is identified.
- [ ] Strata and PSU variables are available.
- [ ] Cross-cycle comparability has been assessed.
- [ ] Analytical limitations are documented.
- [ ] Provenance is preserved.

# Page summary

NHANES laboratory analysis connects:

```text
participant eligibility
specimen collection
laboratory methods
quality assurance
data structure
survey design
reproducibility
```

A released laboratory value becomes defensible analytical evidence only when its scientific, operational, and survey context remain visible throughout the workflow.
